title: Are students as lucky to be here as they feel?
summary: Jim Dickinson tracks how scarcity claims, ceremonial offer letters and gift-framed scholarships convert an ordinary purchase into a debt of gratitude students feel they can't call in
full_text:
I’ve been thinking a lot this summer about rights and confidence.

As I’ve traversed the country delivering training to new SU officers, it’s been rare to hear of student leaders framing themselves as consumers.

But, as the Office for Students (OfS) notes in its consultation on a new condition of registration, they do talk about “fairness” and “honesty’” when they talk about unmet expectations.

New regulation on the nuts and bolts of promises, delivery and complaints may well help. A new single source of information on treating students fairly might help too.

But it was an international student who’d won their election that floored me.

Their journey from Bengaluru to Britain had been fraught with unfairness – outright lies on costs and housing from their agent, a huge and legally unjustifiable deposit, a late arrival and non-existent induction, thin provision marred by strikes, vast class sizes and pitiful support to find a placement.

Despite the myriad issues, she said she nevertheless felt “lucky to be here”.

And the problem with all of the proposals in C6? People who feel lucky to be here suck it up.

Never had it so good

This year, universities and colleges made 1.3 million offers to UK 18-year-olds – up from 1.2 million last year – and 99 per cent of those who applied by the January deadline went into results day holding at least one.

Meanwhile, on the Office for Students’ (OfS) most recent reckoning, 124 English providers – 45 per cent of those analysed – face a deficit in 2025–26 without mitigating action, and nearly one in six are projected to end the year with less than 30 days’ liquidity.

You’d never guess either number from the sector’s Clearing webpages.

At one university, applicants receiving a Clearing offer are invited to “secure your place and choose the reward that fits your student journey” – £500 off first-year accommodation, a £500 tech voucher, or a bundle of “entertainment, food deliveries, shopping perks and career boosting skills” – provided the offer is accepted within 48 hours.

Rewards are limited, allocated first-come first-served, and “all decisions are final”. The reward terminates if you withdraw, requires you to stay enrolled past the census point, and won’t be paid at all if you owe the university money. It’s less a gift, more a device designed to assure continuation. Or “trap you”, as students would call it.

Another’s Clearing FAQs explain that places are “limited” and “generally in high demand”, and that verbal offers are normally held open for 24 hours. One describes Clearing as a “final chance” before moving successful applicants briskly into “You’ve made it” messaging. Another pairs “limited places available on selected courses” with an invitation to “invest in your future”.

Each claim, taken alone, might have an innocent explanation. Taken together, in a cycle where 99 per cent of on-time UK 18-year-old applicants already held an offer and providers are fighting each other for every enrolment, the pattern is harder to explain innocently – a sector whose need for students has rarely been more obvious talks to applicants as though the favour flows the other way.

I’ve taken to calling it “lucky to be here” syndrome – the production of student gratitude and deference by presenting an essentially commercial and mutually dependent relationship as a scarce favour bestowed upon the student by the institution.

Clearing is just where the machinery is easiest to spot in August. The rest of it runs all year round, at every stage of the student lifecycle – and the closer you look, the more the bits represent a system.

Who needs whom

The signature move is a reversal of dependence.

Economically, a university in 2026 is a competing seller that may urgently need tuition income – that’s what the OfS deficit figures mean. Symbolically, it remains the selecting body.

So rather than thinking “this institution worked quite hard to persuade me to buy its provision”, the applicant thinks “this institution judged me worthy of admission” – a contingent power relationship made to feel natural, deserved and almost ceremonial.

And that framing isn’t just an aesthetic choice, because what starts as marketing compounds into something else:

scarce “place” = gift-like “scholarship” = deadline and deposit = offer-holder identity = financial and emotional sunk cost = choice-supportive defence = self-blame and reluctance to complain

The point is not just that universities exaggerate their own desirability – everyone knows that. It’s that prestige can operate as a system of accountability avoidance, cultivated hardest by the institutions that can least afford scrutiny of what the fee actually buys.

The scarcity claim is only the opening gambit, because between offer and enrolment there’s a whole wedge of material designed to convert an unevaluated purchase into an identity.

“Congratulations” arrive before the applicant has had any chance to weigh what they’re being congratulated for. Offer letters carry a vice chancellor’s signature while being sent automatically. Templated messages report that “we saw something special in your application”, and applicants get asked “why this university?” before the university has demonstrated why they should choose it.

One advertises “Exclusive Offer Holder Days” – with limited spaces, naturally, and a prompt to “secure your place now” – where the exclusivity consists of every single offer-holder being invited. Reminds me of the trip to the water park I “won” in Tenerife.

Then come the commitment devices. Offer-holder groups and introductions to “future classmates” build a social world it would now cost something to walk away from. Applicants are encouraged to announce the offer publicly, add the profile-picture frame, choose accommodation, join societies and buy the hoodie – each a small act that raises the emotional price of changing your mind, and each completed before a single seminar can be evaluated.

“Welcome to the family” arrives before a contract has even been formed. The same tricks now run at the retention end too – one page for students considering staying on to postgraduate study pairs an automatic 10 per cent discount with the reassurance “we already know you”.

Congratulations on your automatic scholarship

Think about the sullying of the word “scholarship”. One university offers a “guaranteed scholarship” of £5,000 to eligible self-funding international undergraduates – no competition involved beyond obtaining a place and enrolling.

Another automatically reduces the annual undergraduate fee from £16,000 to £9,790 for eligible students. A university’s Regional Scholarship is an automatic £5,000 off the first year for eligible nationalities, another advertises automatic £10,000 scholarships for postgraduates from Nigeria, and another’s “Global Gold” and “Global Silver” Excellence Scholarships operate as automatic fee discounts on a page that separately offers loyalty and prompt-payment reductions.

One university runs a Loyalty Scholarship – 20 per cent off the first year for eligible returning international students and alumni – alongside a Family Scholarship giving the same reduction to eligible children, grandchildren and siblings of students and alumni, a distinction conferred by kinship with an existing customer.

Another gives graduates, including former exchange students, an automatic 20 per cent “loyalty scholarship”. And a whole family of awards turns out to reward speed of payment rather than anything resembling merit – a £1,500 Early Confirmation Award for unconditional offer-holders who pay by a deadline, a £2,000 discount for international postgraduates who pay their deposit within ten days, an early-acceptance discount, and a £500 early-payment discount – filed, without apparent embarrassment, under “scholarships and waivers”.

The question is what changes when “you qualify for our current price” becomes “we have awarded you a scholarship”. The first framing supports consumer entitlement – you shopped, you compared, you got the going rate. The second creates recognition, gratitude and a relationship with a benefactor, and there’s evidence that the label alone can do purchasing work – scholarship framing shifting enrolment even where net prices were held roughly constant. A discount is something you negotiate. An award is something you live up to.

Top five of a list we compiled ourselves

Scarcity’s twin is prestige, and here at least there’s regulatory history to draw on.

In 2017 the Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) upheld complaints against six universities in one coordinated sweep. One university’s “Top 5 for student satisfaction” had been calculated against a self-selected set of “mainstream” English universities. Another’s “top 1% world university” came without a defensible denominator.

“London’s top modern university” never adequately defined “modern”. Another presented a “No.1 in the UK” physics claim as a REF result when REF ranked no such thing. One university’s “top university in England for long-term graduate prospects” implied more than the particular measure could bear.

ASA rulings aside, the everyday versions are legal and everywhere – whichever league table gives the highest position this year, institutional rank deployed as evidence about a particular course, research rankings offered as evidence of undergraduate teaching quality, Russell Group membership standing in for teaching evidence altogether, “award-winning university” where the award covered one building.

The function is the same as the scarcity claim. The applicant is invited to feel fortunate to be admitted somewhere so demonstrably excellent, on measures that mostly say nothing about what their experience will actually be like.

Then there’s the website’s favourite grammatical trick – the conditional. “Access to placements” can mean students must secure their own. “Placement opportunity” can mean permission to interrupt your studies should you happen to find one. “95 per cent in employment or further study” bundles two outcomes together because one of them is weaker alone, and the employers whose logos decorate a course page may have once attended a careers fair.

A related version inflates the ordinary into the exceptional – “access to academic experts” meaning scheduled teaching, “one-to-one support” meaning one meeting a term, “24/7 support” meaning recorded materials and a chatbot. And the actual valuable things – study abroad, incubators, mentoring schemes, specialist facilities, counselling – get advertised to everyone while being available, competitively, by lottery or via a waiting list, to a few. The words “may”, “can”, “opportunity to” and “access to” do a lot of work.

When it goes wrong, those words turn out to have been the contract. A postgraduate who picked a course largely for its industrial placement, and never got one, was offered half the tuition fee – and the Office of the Independent Adjudicator (OIA) didn’t recommend more, because the published information had offered an “opportunity” rather than a guarantee.

In another case, a provider whose prospectus listed specialist equipment as available from year one – the student couldn’t use it until year three – responded to the complaint by describing its advertised industry access and employment opportunities as “additional services” it wasn’t obliged to deliver. The OIA pointed out that the marketing had made no such distinction, and recommended compensation and a consumer law review.

Independent learning and other savings

Once students are enrolled, the same translation service goes to work on provision itself – and I’ll try to be fair here, because at least some of what I’ve identified below can be perfectly good pedagogy, sincerely delivered. Independent learning is a real thing.

But watch what the language can conceal. Low contact hours become “independent learning” and fewer seminars “build autonomy”. Recorded lectures become “flexible learning” where nobody meaningfully chose flexibility. Merged cohorts become “interdisciplinary learning”, heavy reliance on hourly-paid and inexperienced teachers becomes “practitioner-led” or “near-peer” learning, staff turnover becomes “exposure to diverse perspectives”, delayed marking becomes “rigorous moderation” – and a course closure becomes “portfolio renewal”.

It’s not so much about whether the pedagogical description is flattering. It’s whether it conceals a resource decision the student never got to see, made after they’d already bought in and couldn’t cheaply leave.

Occasionally the curtain slips. In one OIA case concerning a distance-learning course that lacked promised practical content and suffered chronic staff unavailability, internal documents showed staff saying they could not support the number of students being recruited. The OIA upheld the complaint, required quality and marketing reviews, and informed OfS.

You get out what you put in

Then when a student notices the gap between the brochure and the provision, another vocab appears – partnership.

Student charters present symmetrical obligations between an individual teenager and a large corporate institution. Poor outcomes get explained through engagement, attendance becomes the standard answer to dissatisfaction with teaching, difficulty with fragmented services becomes evidence of inadequate independence, and predictable structural problems – overload, insecure housing, timetable chaos – get met with “resilience” language and a referral to wellbeing services.

Students are partners when it’s time to co-produce and consumers when it’s time to pay, while “professionalism” requirements police the tone of criticism rather than its substance. Watch how the institution’s account of the relationship shifts depending on which description is most advantageous at any given moment:

MomentThe university appears asThe student becomes RecruitmentDesirable sellerA customer to be won AdmissionSelective gatekeeperA fortunate supplicant Fee reductionGenerous benefactorA grateful award-holder Weak provisionSetter of legitimate academic expectationsAn insufficiently engaged learner ComplaintAuthoritative academic bodyA potentially entitled troublemaker League table seasonSuccessful institutionEvidence of institutional success

When you’re being recruited, you’re an empowered chooser. When provision is weak, you may hear about your engagement. When you demand redress, you risk reclassification as a consumerist troublemaker. And when the rankings come out, you’re the evidence. The recurring asymmetry underneath is simple – success validates the institution, failure tests the student.

Defending the purchase

The psychology stacking the deck is mostly well established, if rarely assembled in one place. Aronson and Mills demonstrated in 1959 that the more severe the initiation, the more people value the group they’ve joined – and an admissions cycle of personal statements, interviews, offer-holder days, deposits and moving house is a perfectly serviceable initiation rite.

Choice-supportive bias means people misremember their chosen option as better than it was, and higher education adds an incentive most purchases lack – because the seller’s reputation prices the qualification, publicly devaluing your university feels like devaluing your own certificate. Complaining about the product means talking down your own asset.

Gratitude on its own doesn’t need to suppress anything – grateful people complain all the time. Indebtedness is the more accurate description, because it implies obligation – they did something for me, so I shouldn’t behave disloyally.

A discount framed as an award manufactures that – a social relationship with a benefactor, in place of a transparent one between buyer and seller. And the machinery openly recruits students into maintaining the asset – telling them that NSS participation protects the value of their degree, treating public criticism as ammunition for rivals, selecting the enthusiastic for recruitment panels and paying student influencers to perform an aspirational version of the experience their coursemates are actually having.

The same message also hit differently for different students. A confident applicant from a graduate family may hear “they competed to recruit me – I have leverage”. A first-generation student may hear “they took a chance on me – I must prove I deserve to stay”.

For international students the indebtedness comes with teeth, because teaching, immigration sponsorship, accommodation, references and sometimes scholarship-renewal conditions all run through the same institution – and it’s worse for doctoral students, dependent on a supervisor for progression, funding, authorship, networks and examination, for whom the cost of voice can be a career.

The variable that matters is whether belonging feels secure (“I belong here, so I have a right to challenge it”) or conditional (“my membership was a favour, and criticism might prove I never deserved it”).

Grateful people don’t ask for refunds

Once you’ve seen it once, you see it everywhere. “The provision is inadequate” becomes “perhaps I’m not engaging properly”. “The course didn’t deliver what was promised” becomes “maybe university is just supposed to be difficult”. A demand becomes an apologetic query, postponed until marks, references or visas are safe – and the student defends the university to outsiders while slating it anonymously on Reddit.

The OIA’s caseload shows what awaits those who push through anyway. Students who chose a postgraduate course because it was advertised as professionally accredited discovered after enrolment that accreditation had ended – staff informally accepted the information was wrong, the formal process still required students to prove they’d been misled, and an initial £500 offer became a full fee refund plus £5,000 only after the OIA got involved.

Around the formal cases there’s the everyday architecture of containment – procedures buried several clicks deep, informal conversations required before anything is recorded, cohort-wide problems divided into individual cases with no group route, short deadlines for students and leisurely ones for institutions, compensation described as “goodwill”, settlements with confidentiality terms attached – and “you said, we did” campaigns that fix the microwaves and the library hours while staffing goes untouched.

The Competition and Markets Authority’s compliance review of the undergraduate sector found contract and complaint terms that could act as barriers to complaining at all, and it extracted commitments from named providers – on terms that gave broad discretion to alter courses, and on the practice of withholding graduation, certificates and re-enrolment over unrelated non-tuition debts.

So when a provider points to low complaint numbers as evidence of satisfaction, remember what a formal complaint requires – picking the right procedural category, contemporaneous evidence, short deadlines, complaining first to the people you’re complaining about, and persistence while the institution in question continues to mark your work, write your references and sometimes sponsor your visa.

A formally fair process still converts a collectively experienced institutional problem into a quasi-legal individual case. Low complaint volume is compatible with excellent provision – and equally compatible with highly effective gratitude framing.

Put the whole cycle together and it looks like this:

manufacture scarcity = confer recognition = secure commitment = obscure provision = transfer responsibility = capture voice = recruit students into defending the credential

Publish the denominator

Some scarcity is real – research supervisors have finite capacity, clinical and placement-based courses carry genuine caps, and “limited places” on those pages describes an actual constraint.

And none of what I’m describing needs a villain – conversion targets, ceremonial tradition and ambient consumer psychology can produce the whole effect between them without anyone ever sitting down to plan the suppression of complaints.

The trouble is that from where an applicant sits, genuine rationing and ordinary sales urgency look identical – and a sector both desperate for cash and with the ASA, CMA and OIA record above doesn’t get to claim a presumption of innocence.

OfS’ current student protection proposals set up misleading marketing, pressurised recruitment and the discouraging of complaints as regulatory red lines – which sets up an obvious early test.

Is “secure your place in the next 48 hours”, from a provider forecasting a deficit, pressurised recruitment – or just how the market talks now? A sector that made 1.3 million offers to school leavers while telling all of them to hurry ought to find that question uncomfortable. Whether the regulator finds it easy will tell us plenty.

full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Professor Rosa Wells, Deputy Vice-Chancellor (Further Education, Apprenticeships and STEM), University College Birmingham.

The timing could hardly have been more appropriate. As educators, employers and policymakers gathered at Warwick Manufacturing Group for the inaugural forum of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers’ Engineering Educators Community, the Government announced plans to introduce new technical pathways for young people from the age of 14.

From September 2028, pupils would be able to combine core academic subjects with technical education connected to local industries, workplace experience and employers. Discussions throughout the forum suggested that the direction of travel was widely welcomed for those seeking careers in engineering.

However, introducing technical pathways at 14 will not, by itself, create a coherent technical education system. The policy must also address what happens next.

The missing middle

Too often, progression is presented as a choice between an apprenticeship and a three-year degree. Both are valuable, but this binary choice overlooks Higher Technical Education at Levels 4 and 5, including Higher National Certificates, Higher National Diplomas and Foundation Degrees already offered by many providers.

This is the ‘missing middle’ in England’s skills system. The Government’s own Post-16 education and skills white paper acknowledges that too few people choose to study at Levels 4 and 5, despite positive economic returns and growing employer demand for these skills. The latest Skills England assessment similarly concludes that the UK compares well internationally at degree level but ranks sixth among G7 countries for the proportion of adults whose highest qualification is at Level 4 or 5.

Awareness is part of the problem. Young people and their parents are generally familiar with degrees and increasingly understand degree apprenticeships. Higher Technical Education has a much weaker public identity. Unless the new school pathways make the full range of progression opportunities visible, they could increase engagement in technical education at 14 without increasing access to higher levels of learning.

The pathways should therefore be designed backwards from the skilled occupations the economy needs. Pupils should be able to see how technical study at school can lead to college, an apprenticeship, Higher Technical Education and, where appropriate, a degree and professional recognition. These should not be separate routes with difficult transition points, but connected stages through which people can enter, leave and return to learning.

Build on existing networks

Schools have already made significant progress in careers education and employer engagement through the Gatsby Benchmarks. However, they cannot be expected to create specialist technical provision, communicate every progression route and develop deep relationships across complex industries alone.

Nor should each school have to negotiate separately with employers that already face numerous requests for engagement. This is particularly difficult for smaller engineering businesses, which may have valuable expertise but limited capacity to offer apprenticeships or sustain relationships with multiple institutions.

The Government should use established regional partnerships to coordinate this activity. Unless Careers Hubs and Regional Access Partnerships can prioritise technical education pathways, it will fall to providers themselves to co-ordinate activity. Further education colleges, universities, University Technical Colleges, Institutes of Technology, Technical Excellence Colleges and employer groups already hold much of the necessary expertise, equipment and industry relationships.

Institutes of Technology illustrate what this can look like. They bring together further and higher education with employers to develop higher-level technical skills through specialist facilities and industry-informed provision.

Collaborative projects have also allowed further education college learners to work alongside undergraduates on Industry 4.0 challenges. Elsewhere, specialist Higher National Certificate programmes enable employees from different parts of the electrical power sector, for example, to study and learn from one another.

The purpose of highlighting these examples is not to argue for a single institutional model. It is to show that the foundations for connected technical pathways already exist. Policy should make better use of them rather than create another layer of structures.

Three priorities for implementation

First, progression to Levels 4 and 5 should be built explicitly into the design of the new pathways. Information about Higher Technical Qualifications should be included in careers guidance, teacher development and communications with parents, alongside degrees and apprenticeships.

Second, schools should be connected systematically to regional technical education networks. These could coordinate access to specialist facilities, employer projects, workplace experiences and professional development for teachers and careers advisers. This would reduce duplication and make employer participation more manageable, particularly for smaller businesses.

Third, success should be measured through progression as well as participation. Evaluation should examine whether learners continue into relevant further education, apprenticeships and Higher Technical Education and not simply how many pupils take a technical option at 14. Destinations at Levels 4 and 5 should be visible within the policy’s accountability measures.

The Government’s proposals offer an important opportunity to give technical education greater status and visibility. But starting earlier will achieve little if young people still encounter fragmented routes and limited information as they progress.

The goal should not simply be more technical education in schools. It should be a connected system in which young people can see and move through the full pathway from initial interest to higher technical skills and professional careers.

full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Professor James Miller FRSE, Co-Commissioner of the Futures Framework.

Public policy rarely suffers from a shortage of opinions. What is often missing is a shared understanding of the evidence.

That is why the publication of A Funding Gap Analysis of Scotland’s University Sector is such an important moment. It represents the first comprehensive, evidence-led assessment of the financial sustainability of Scotland’s universities for many years and, significantly, it was co-commissioned by Universities Scotland and the Scottish Government through the Future Framework for the Sustainability and Success of Scotland’s Universities.

In itself, that collaboration is historic.

At a time when debates about higher education can become polarised between institutional interests, political positions and competing narratives, the Future Framework has brought together government, universities, trade unions, student representatives, funding bodies and independent experts around a common purpose: establishing the facts. The report led by Professor Sir Anton Muscatelli provides a shared evidence base from which future policy discussions can proceed.

The findings are undoubtedly challenging. The analysis concludes that Scottish universities face a growing structural funding gap. Publicly funded teaching does not recover its full cost. Research, despite its enormous contribution to Scotland’s economy and society, is also funded below full economic cost. Over time, universities have become increasingly reliant on international student income to support teaching, research, innovation and infrastructure. In 2023/24 alone, the report identifies an estimated sector-wide funding gap of around £200 million. TRAC data for Scotland in 2024/25 is due out imminently, and there is every expectation that it will show a widening of the gap.

These findings deserve serious attention. But they do not justify simplistic conclusions.

Indeed, one of the report’s greatest strengths is that it deliberately avoids recommending specific solutions. Its purpose was diagnostic, not prescriptive. The task was to understand the scale and nature of the challenge rather than advocate for a particular policy outcome. The next phases of the Future Framework, which are already underway, will build on this evidence before options for the future are developed.

That distinction matters because higher education is a complex system. Universities are not simply teaching providers. They educate future workers, generate research and innovation, support public services, drive economic growth, strengthen communities and act as anchor institutions within their regions. The report illustrates how interconnected these activities have become and how funding flows between them in ways that are often poorly understood by those outside the sector.

The temptation now will be to move quickly from diagnosis to predetermined solutions. Some will argue for increased public investment. Others will focus on efficiency, reform or diversification of income. Still others may question aspects of the current system itself.

Yet the evidence suggests the reality is more complicated than any single narrative permits.

The challenges facing Scotland’s universities vary across institutional missions, geographies and funding models. The needs of research-intensive institutions are not identical to those with a stronger regional or professional focus. Equally, the interests of students, staff, employers and government must all be considered. The choices ahead will involve trade-offs, and none should be approached lightly.

If there is one lesson to take from this report, it is that future policy should be guided by the same evidence-based approach that produced it. Assumptions should be tested. Consequences should be evaluated. Easy answers should be treated with caution.

The challenges facing Scotland’s universities are real and significant. But so too is the achievement of producing a shared, credible evidence base across such a wide range of stakeholders.

The next phases will be more difficult. The options will be contested. The decisions may be uncomfortable.

But Scotland is now in a far better position to make those decisions because it has started with the evidence rather than the ideology. And that is precisely where good public policy begins.

full_text:
The crisis in the youth employment market, with almost a million young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) across the UK, has placed fresh emphasis on ways of getting employees into the workforce.

The government hopes to increase focus on technical and vocational learning in England from the age of 14. In parallel, there is an ambition to create thousands more apprenticeships.

The work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden, has also announced a new bursary aimed at ensuring families will not be left financially worse off if their teenager starts an apprenticeship.

Research from the National Foundation for Educational Research (NFER) found that black and mixed-ethnicity learners from poorer backgrounds and those for whom English is an additional language are less likely to complete their apprenticeships.

The Guardian asked people to share their experiences of apprenticeships.

‘I am progressing faster than colleagues with degrees’

Ellen*, 24, from Worcester, decided an apprenticeship would work better for her than university, although it was “never suggested” as an option at school.

“It was just assumed that uni was going to be the way I went,” she says. “I did my own research on my other options.”

Securing an apprenticeship was not easy, and she experienced “a lot of rejections” before she won a place at a medium-sized MEP (mechanical, electrical and plumbing) consultancy.

Her three-year apprenticeship was four days a week with a day at college for her higher national certificate (HNC) studies. Her HNC course was two years, but the apprenticeship requirement of submitting evidence added an additional year.

Ellen passed, gaining a BTec level 4 HNC as well as a CIBSE (Chartered Institute of Building Services Engineers) Licentiate, and EngTech certification through CIBSE as an end-point assessment organisation and the UK regulatory body, the Engineering Council.

“It was a huge learning curve and I had to ask for extra help from my teachers,” she says. “At 18, being thrown into the deep end, you just want to do well, you just want to try your best to get all the answers right.

“I had a really good experience at the company that took me on as an apprentice and then gave me a job – really supportive managers – but I found it difficult to balance work, study and having a social life. All my friends chose to go to university and were all over the country, and there was no one around my age at work so having any social life was very difficult.”

Ellen says a “lack of female role models” within her industry and office was also “a difficulty”.

“I have since moved into fire sprinkler design, but starting my new career with a construction qualification and four years of industry experience has meant I am progressing faster than my colleagues who have degrees,” she says.

‘I was effectively being paid to learn’

Harry, 26, a machinist, says he feels “gratitude” that he has a job, as he sees friends who went to university now questioning that decision.

“Some have needed uni to get the jobs that they have now, but some of them I don’t think have needed it, and they’re starting to realise that,” he says.

Harry, from Billingshurst, West Sussex, says that, after achieving three A-levels, he briefly flirted with the idea of studying business at university.

“The cost put me off,” he says. “Also, it didn’t sit right with me in my gut to go to university. I just didn’t think I had the mental strength for full-time education while balancing a part-time job and watching my money.”

Instead, he worked two ski seasons as a chaperone in France and was planning a third when the Covid pandemic closed down tourism.

“I was lucky and privileged enough to be able to come back home to stay with my family,” he says. “They obviously wanted me to get a job to pay rent.”

Harry knew about apprenticeships through his father, who had done an electrician’s apprenticeship in the late 1980s, and applied for “about five”. He got a four-year level 3 engineering machine technician work placement, involving a day a week of study. He started his apprenticeship in 2020, but delays due to Covid meant he finished it in 2025.

Harry threw himself into his studies. “While I was at college, I made sure that all the time I was there, I was doing as much work as I could because I was effectively being paid to learn,” he says.

At the end of his apprenticeship, he gained an engineering technician (machinist – advanced manufacturing engineering) level 3 qualification. The apprenticeship had a guaranteed job if he passed. Harry was offered a role, but he decided to go elsewhere for a better wage.

He adds: “I do take gratitude in the fact that I have a job. People are meant to come out of uni and find a career, but I don’t think many of them can.”

‘Some people were not ready to come to work’

Hannah*, a metalworker, says while her apprenticeship was “amazing”, she saw how others struggled and missed out on completing theirs because of a lack of support.

“The work suited me, and I received plenty of affirmation after a long spell of unemployment and low self-confidence,” she says. “The college qualification opened a lot of doors.

“I took maths and English functional skills tests as part of the process, having not taken any exams as a school-refusing teenager, but the course had some shortcomings when it came to material and delivery – my cohort on the course were almost universally disengaged.”

Hannah, who is in her 30s and lives in south-west England, dropped out of school aged 14, only returning sporadically. She was “in that category of Neet for quite a while”, turning to the apprenticeship after periods in college, cleaning part-time and picking up “little bits of work” in her 20s.

While she is encouraged by the government’s plans regarding technical learning and apprenticeships, she sounds a note of caution. Hannah saw several people unable to continue with their apprenticeship and believes more guided support would have helped, adding that some of the cohort “struggled with attendance and emotional regulation”.

“I think apprenticeships can be fantastic, but they aren’t the panacea for joblessness,” she says. “There’s a lot of really good intentions to try and use the apprenticeship programme to get people who might have been a bit like me, though I was also very privileged because I had a supportive family and wasn’t from a really deprived background.

“But I saw some people on the apprenticeship, particularly the younger ones, who were just not ready to come into work. Some of them had quite complex emotional problems or difficult backgrounds as well, which makes it even harder.”

‘Not having any debt is very freeing’

Jotham, 24, from Buckinghamshire, says he regarded his three-year degree apprenticeship as the “safest route” to securing a job.

“I knew before I did my A-levels that I wanted to do an apprenticeship,” he says. “My dad had said it was a good option and I looked at the government list. University was a backup option if it hadn’t worked out.”

He applied for “about 20 to 30 apprenticeships” and chose a scheme with one day a week studying at university in London that meant he could live at home and commute. It started in 2019.

“The company I chose had two apprentices at the same time, so that was an advantage, as you had someone to do it with, and the previous apprentice was also there and would help us,” he says.

He achieved a first in his digital and technology solutions apprenticeship BSc. Although there was no guarantee of a job at the end of his course, Jotham “carried on working at the same place and was offered a job”.

“It’s a very practical option, isn’t it?” he says. “It has all of the advantages of university and none of the disadvantages. Not having any debt is very freeing.”

However, he knew of some apprentices who were not so lucky: one had to stop “a year in” because the firm collapsed.

“Others either had to stop completely or change how they did the course because the company wasn’t able to employ them for the whole three years,” he adds. “That was a lot of bother for them, because there was no backup plan built into the course.”

Jotham is now working in database management.

“In the job market, really what’s wanted is experience, but people coming out of their degree may struggle to get that,” he says. “With an apprenticeship, you get the experience. The degree is almost like a checkbox item.”

*Names have been changed

full_text:
A house near a top state secondary school costs an extra £40,000 on average, according to research that reveals education premiums that rank alongside some private school fees.

The average property in a postcode district that includes a top 50 state secondary commands a price tag of £415,791, compared with £375,217 across the wider local authority areas in which those schools are located, a UK-wide analysis by the estate agent Yopa found.

The £40,574 extra, a premium of about 11%, can be compared with an average annual fee of £23,000 charged by private schools, according to the Good Schools Guide.

However, some charge less than £6,000 a year, indicating that over seven years of secondary education parents could end up paying a similar sum to the average extra cost of a house near a top state school.

The increased price tag for such properties varies significantly across the country, according to the research, although individual cases can be less informative than the overall average, due to local market factors.

Bishop Vesey’s grammar school in the well-to-do West Midlands town of Sutton Coldfield tops the table of schools where buyers are likely to pay much more than in the surrounding area.

Homes across the B74 postcode district go for an average of £509,964, a premium of £275,814 compared with the average of £234,150 in Birmingham, which includes more economically deprived areas.

In London, the biggest premium is paid by people living close to Henrietta Barnett school, a grammar academy for girls. The average property across its NW11 postcode is valued at 37% more than in the rest of the surrounding borough of Barnet, equivalent to an additional £354,288.

However, there are some outliers to the trend. Across the postcode district home to Reading school and Kendrick school, the average property costs £276,870. That is £84,373 below the wider Reading average of £361,243.

Verona Frankish, the chief executive of Yopa, said: “For many homebuyers with children, the quality of local schools is one of the most important considerations when deciding where to live and, with the new school year approaching, education will be front of mind for many families considering their next move.”

Separate research reveals that in London, homebuyers with children who go to a nearby private school are opting in to a double whammy of extra costs, with properties near a top fee-paying establishment – which are often located in the most upmarket areas – going for premiums of up to 77%.

Queen’s college, London, tops the table. Homes across the W1 postcode command an average price of £1.92m compared with the wider Westminster average of £854,198.

Westminster school and Francis Holland school, Sloane Square follow. Both are located within the SW1 postcode, where the average property price stands at £1.49m, a premium of 54.5% compared with Westminster as a whole.

title: Valuing Black Studies Requires Valuing Black People. Few Institutions Do.
summary:
Valuing Black Studies Requires Valuing Black People. Few Institutions Do.
Sara Brady Mon, 08/31/2026 - 03:00 AM

Defunding or altogether eliminating Black studies will surely exacerbate racialized persistence and experiential and student outcomes inequities on predominantly white campuses.

Byline(s)
Shaun Harper
full_text:
Reporters, radio show hosts and podcasters have reached out in recent days asking to talk with me about the state of Black studies programs and departments on campuses across the country. “Universities that have closed or merged African American studies units over the past two years include the University of Iowa, the University of Texas at Austin and the University of Kansas,” Todd Wallack wrote in a Washington Post article last week. “Others have eliminated or begun phasing out majors and degrees, including Kennesaw State University, the University of Toledo and Indiana University at Bloomington. Several colleges have also trimmed classes, removed them from the core curriculum or cut staff.”

Wallack notes that declining enrollments, the anti-DEI policy environment and federal budget cuts to higher education are being used to justify the elimination of Black studies programs: “U.S. colleges awarded fewer than 700 African American Studies degrees in each of the past three years, the lowest levels in two decades.” This is indeed alarming. Could enrollment declines be explained, at least in part, by insufficient institutional efforts to attract student applicants to Black studies? Could it be that too few colleges and universities value Black studies enough to strategically showcase it as one of the most important academic offerings on campus? Or might it be that enrollment declines signal something bigger: an undervaluing of anything and everything in higher education—except big-time revenue-generating sports—that involves Black students and employees?

“This university does not care about Black people” is one of the strongest and most recurring appraisals that Black students, faculty and staff offer during interviews for my qualitative campus climate studies. For years, students have named Black studies courses, along with Black culture centers, as the only sites on campus that offer affirmation, cultivate sense of belonging and provide culturally relevant learning opportunities. Accordingly, these are spaces where Black students recover from “onlyness’ (being the only one or one of only a few Black people in almost all their courses), microaggressions and overt encounters with racism on campus.

Defunding or altogether eliminating Black studies will surely exacerbate racialized persistence and experiential and student outcomes inequities on predominantly white campuses. Black students will be most negatively affected, which will delight white supremacists and others who do not believe that Black people actually deserve to be admitted to or employed by colleges and universities that were never designed with us in mind.

Consider a racially stratified institution where the overwhelming majority of Black professionals work in food service, groundskeeping and custodial positions; where Black people are terribly underrepresented in professorships, directorships, deanships and executive leadership roles; where Eurocentric content and ways of knowing continually pervade the curriculum; where white students and employees get away with calling Black people the N-word without consequence; and where Black people routinely encounter racist stereotypes, racial profiling and at times racial violence on campus. It should surprise no one that Black studies is not valued at those places. I am acknowledging, not normalizing or excusing any of this.

The devaluing of Black studies is persistent and pervasive, not new. The field emerged first and foremost from the brilliance of Black writers, teachers and thinkers. Its formal creation and multiplication on campuses across the country are attributable to student protests throughout the 1960s at Merritt College, San Francisco State College and elsewhere. Black student activists and allies demanded the creation of courses, curricula and full academic programs where everyone (including, but not limited to Black collegians) could learn about Black history and culture. Institutions resisted. Many invested the bare minimum into infrastructure, physical spaces and faculty hires for the earliest Black studies programs. In most places, that never changed. Black studies has always had to fight for its life and operate without sufficient resources.

For myriad reasons, my love for Black studies is deeply personal. I highlight a half dozen herein. First, I have been Black for 50 years. I love Black people, history and culture enough to demand inclusion. Giving us scraps has never been acceptable to me. Second, I love America enough to insist that its full truths be taught and learned, including what it did and still does to Black people. I want these truths to be rigorously taught and learned across the curriculum. But Black studies is the place I trust most for such curricular consistency and integrity. To be sure, I want both: Black studies departments and the teaching of Black topics everywhere else.

Third, I love very smart people. Many on last week’s list of A-plus Black scholars teach in Black studies at elite postsecondary institutions. Many more teach at historically Black colleges and universities, including the one from which I proudly graduated. During my decade on the University of Pennsylvania faculty, one of my three appointments was in Africana studies. Some of the smartest people I have ever met were my colleagues there. I am a proud member of the Black Studies Center here at the University of Southern California. Because the faculty scholarship is so extraordinary and because we do the outsize work of exposing USC students across all racial groups to Black content that prepares them for work and citizenship in a racially diverse democracy, ours really should be a department—at very least, a full academic program.

Fourth, I am a lover of interdisciplinarity. By design, Black studies is deeply and impressively interdisciplinary. Colleges and universities that claim to value interdisciplinarity ought to recognize Black studies as a constant exemplar that deserves more, not fewer resources. Fifth, I love colleagues and academic units that do what I called “accepting educational responsibility” in my American Educational Research Association presidential address. Many people misunderstand Black studies to be only for Black students. On the contrary, Black studies faculty have always accepted responsibility for ensuring that all students—including Asian Americans, Latinos, Native Americans and whites—do not go into workplaces and societies with racist, inadequate and anti-Black misunderstandings of who Black people are.

The sixth reason I highlight here is most important: I love Black elders and greatly value enduring treasures they left behind. Black studies is one of those treasures. Black Americans fought for the creation of Black studies in the 1960s. They and others continued fighting throughout the ’70s, ’80s, ’90s and 2000s. I love them for never giving up and for refusing to be pushed off campuses. Generations of Black scholars give me hope during these outrageous times. As has always been the case, it will be Black people who fight for and ultimately save Black studies. I will continue doing my part to ensure that these programs and departments, as well as Black people within and beyond them, are valued in higher education.

title: UNC Ends Study Abroad Program in China
summary:
UNC Ends Study Abroad Program in China
sara.custer@in… Mon, 08/31/2026 - 03:00 AM
Byline(s)
Sara Custer
full_text:
The University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill has ended a study abroad program with Fudan University in China “out of an abundance of caution” after the Department of Defense ordered the university to review relationships with foreign institutions that it says could be a threat to national security.

In a letter shared with The Daily Tarheel to Joseph S. Sewell, the DOD assistant secretary for science and technology, UNC Chancellor Lee Roberts said the institution reviewed the scope of its relationship with Fudan after the Shanghai-based institution was added to the department’s Section 1286 list of “foreign institutions engaging in problematic activities” at the end of July.

“The identified relationship was a study-abroad program for undergraduate students and was unrelated to research activities, including sensitive research, Department of War-funded research or export-controlled research,” Roberts wrote. “Out of an abundance of caution, UNC decided on August 12, 2026 to cancel the study-abroad program with Fudan University.”

UNC students take courses taught in English at Fudan’s School of Social Development and Public Policy and its International Summer School. The partnership was first proposed in 2013 and renewed in 2022. A university spokesperson told The News & Observer that four UNC students currently studying at Fudan are not affected and will finish their semester abroad.

UNC is among 30 institutions the DOD directed this month to audit their partnerships with foreign institutions. The agency gave each university until the end of the month to submit its findings and terminate any relationships found to be “problematic,” the department said. Any university that does not comply could lose federal research funding.

In the letter sent to Sewell, Roberts said UNC’s Research Security program had identified two unfunded research projects with two other Chinese partners: one between researchers at Harbin Institute of Technology and a faculty member at UNC’s Kenan-Flagler Business School and another between researchers at Shanghai Jiao Tong University and a faculty member in the School of Data Science and Society.

Roberts said both partnerships are in their final stages and “neither project has received or involves any federal funding, and neither overlaps with any federally sponsored research activities at the University.”

“The faculty involved are committed solely to completing their publication work and have agreed to fully terminate these relationships upon doing so,” Roberts wrote.

title: How Accreditation Changes Could Impact Professional Licensure
summary:
How Accreditation Changes Could Impact Professional Licensure
jessica.blake@… Mon, 08/31/2026 - 03:00 AM

As more accreditors opt out of federal recognition or risk having it stripped, some programs and practitioners face mounting uncertainty over what it means for licensing requirements.

Byline(s)
Jessica Blake
full_text:
President Trump’s proposal to strip the American Bar Association’s accreditation arm of its gatekeeping powers for federal student aid has triggered a cascade of questions and concerns about whether future law school graduates in certain states will be able to obtain an attorney’s license.

Legal and higher ed experts say it will come down to each state’s licensure rules and what, if anything, those rules say about whether practitioners are required to graduate from a law school accredited by a federally recognized agency. But at a time when accreditation is becoming increasingly politicized and volatile, the complex relationship between state licensure regulations and the Education Department’s recognition of accreditors is being tested, they say, creating a sense of uncertainty.

Moreover, lawyers aren’t the only ones facing questions about licensure. Similar concerns have emerged for other professions—especially those related to health care, which may be at even more risk of licensing challenges in the ever-shifting landscape of quality control.

Just a few weeks before the ABA announcement, the Midwifery Education Accreditation Council—the only accreditor for midwifery programs that don’t require students to have prior nursing education—announced that it had voluntarily opted out of federal recognition. The move sparked anxiety about whether direct-entry midwives would be able to obtain a license.

Such fears may soon become more common across other professions: Experts say the number of federally recognized accreditors will likely decrease more, whether by force or by choice. The Education Department is attempting to overhaul the expectations set on each accreditor, programmatic as well as institutional, and the department’s advisory committee has been voting to crack down on the agencies it says aren’t meeting existing standards. Both shifts could lead to a host of conflicts with licensing criteria for the programs and practitioners that depend on that recognition for their livelihood.

“Anyone who’s working with licensed professions should pay attention to what’s happening,” said Robert Shireman, a member of ED’s accreditation advisory board. Many professions are “not in any way linked to federal recognition,” Shireman added, but for those that are, “there could be some snags.”

Which Programs Are at Risk?

Higher education is governed by two kinds of accreditors, programmatic—those that assess the quality of a particular type of program, department or school—and institutional, which evaluate entire institutions. Both types can choose to apply for federal recognition, which would allow them to decide whether an institution can access federal student grants and loans, but they don’t have to. And the Education Department, which decides whether an accreditor is federally recognized, has no control over the licensure of degree earners. That’s determined at the state level by the Legislature or a board and can differ for each profession.

Some state statutes say that in order to qualify for a license in a specific profession, an individual has to have earned their degree from a college or university accredited by a particular programmatic accreditor. For example, to become a licensed occupational therapist in California, one must graduate from a college accredited by the American Occupational Therapy Association’s Accreditation Council for Occupational Therapy Education.

In those cases, federal recognition of the accreditor is not a concern because even if it were to withdraw from or be denied the Education Department’s seal of approval, it could continue to accredit colleges; students at those institutions just wouldn’t be eligible for federal aid unless they also have an institutional accreditor. As long as a college is accredited, graduates in those states can qualify for a license.

But if a state’s regulations say that an individual must graduate from a college accredited by a federally recognized accreditor, then it could become a problem. In those cases, if an institution is accredited only by a programmatic accreditor and that accreditor withdraws from or loses its federal recognition, then its graduates would no longer be able to obtain a license in that state unless the institution found a new accreditor.

When it comes to legal licenses, the ABA’s accreditation council says that only one state requires federal recognition—Florida.

But even in that case, the effect of the ABA’s potential loss of federal recognition appears to be minimal. The Florida Supreme Court order says that in order to qualify for the bar exam, a student must graduate from a college accredited by “a programmatic accrediting agency recognized by the United States Department of Education to accredit programs in legal education” or “an institutional accrediting agency recognized by the United States Department of Education to accredit institutions of higher education, provided the institutional accrediting agency is also approved by the Court.”

Nationally, five stand-alone law schools rely solely on the ABA for accreditation, and at this point their graduates will not qualify for Florida licensure if ABA’s recognition is denied. But 183 of the law schools affiliated with the ABA are part of a larger university, so they have a second and broader institutional accreditor; what remains unclear is whether those institutional accreditors will be approved by the Florida Supreme Court and if they will have to set new programmatic standards specific to J.D.s in order to do so. (Nine stand-alone schools that are not part of a larger university have also hired a second accreditor.)

Earning a license in midwifery may be harder. Unlike the Education Department’s proposal to deny ABA recognition—which must still be finalized—MEAC’s decision to opt out of recognition was voluntary. And multiple midwifery schools told Inside Higher Ed that the accreditor’s decision was made without consulting all member institutions and that it came without warning, leaving little time for the schools to come up with a plan.

The MEAC’s statement explaining the withdrawal says little to address concerns about licensure other than that it will be “monitoring state-level licensure statutes.” Inside Higher Ed reached out for further comment, but MEAC declined to respond.

Licensure access may also be more uncertain for midwives—especially those without a foundational nursing degree—because the practice isn’t allowed in every state. Only 38 states provide direct-entry licenses, according to the North American Registry of Midwives.

It’s unclear exactly how many states require a federally recognized accreditor for graduates to obtain a midwifery license. But Shireman said it would make sense if they did; in less traditional health-care professions, proving the existence of a federally recognized programmatic accreditor can often be key to lobbying for state-level clearance, he said.

“It sounds meaningful to say that you are a federally recognized accreditor or that you are designated by the U.S. Department of Education as an accrediting body,” he explained—though “it sounds more meaningful than it really is.”

Inside Higher Ed reached out to five of the 11 MEAC-accredited institutions. Three said they are concerned about their graduates’ ability to obtain a license, and two of those said they are actively seeking a second accreditor that is federally recognized. The other two said they are either located in a state that doesn’t require federal recognition or are part of a larger university with a federally recognized institutional accreditor.

Vicki Penwell, co-founder of Mercy in Action College of Midwifery, a direct-entry midwife school that serves students in 34 states through distance learning, said she has been in numerous meetings since MEAC announced its withdrawal to try to find a way to protect her students.

Both Idaho, where the college is based, and NC SARA, the group that streamlines regulations for online college programs across state lines, require federal recognition. So unless Penwell and her team can find a new accreditor by the end of the year, she will have to stop instructing her online students. And if she hasn’t found one by next June, she’ll have to drop her in-state learners as well.

“When MEAC withdrew, no one from the member schools was on board. We would have changed everything if we knew—we could have tried to help problem-solve and address the issues that MEAC said it was withdrawing for,” Penwell said. “The cautionary tale in my mind is that for the people who write the licensure policies and laws, it’s a bad idea to name a particular accreditor and maybe they shouldn’t be naming the Department of Education [and the requirement of federal recognition], either.”

License Challenges

Some critics have questioned why a programmatic accreditor would voluntarily withdraw in the first place. But the Association of Specialized and Professional Accreditors, an advocacy group for programmatic accreditors, put out a statement earlier this week saying that for some, the sacrifices and costs required to qualify for federal recognition may not be worth it, since “federal recognition is not accreditation.”

“A federal link is important where it serves a purpose—but it is not what creates an accreditor, nor is it the only measure of an accreditor’s mission, authority, standards, value, rigor, and outcomes,” the statement reads.

In a follow-up email to Inside Higher Ed, ASPA’s executive director, Zach Waymer, said that concerns about access to professional licenses are valid but driven largely by states, not the programmatic accreditors.

When state laws require federal recognition, “that state and its licensing authority will likely need to determine how the provision applies when an accreditor voluntarily relinquishes federal recognition but continues to accredit programs,” Waymer wrote.

Education Under Secretary Nicholas Kent made a similar comment in June when he opted to give the Council on Naturopathic Medical Education one last chance to get in line before stripping its federal recognition. In a letter, Kent said he found the argument that losing federal recognition would “create immediate and measurable disruption” to licensure access and workforce entry “unpersuasive.”

“It must be stated clearly that no accreditor is exempt from the possibility of loss of recognition. If CNME, or any similarly situated accreditor, is concerned about the potential impact of termination on graduates of its accredited programs, it should work with relevant state authorities and the broader profession to mitigate any such effects,” he wrote. “I will not be compelled to continue recognizing a noncompliant accreditor based solely on how an industry has chosen to structure itself.”

Other key programmatic accreditors and their institutional members could soon find themselves confronted with similar decisions.

The Council on Chiropractic Education said it sent a letter to the presidents of its member institutions saying it voted to “begin a process of withdrawal,” weighing risks like licensure eligibility, though nothing has been finalized. And the National Accrediting Commission of Career Arts and Sciences—one of the nation’s largest cosmetology and massage therapy accreditors—may soon lose its recognition involuntarily once Kent makes a final decision. The Education Department’s advisory committee voted 9 to 3 in favor of rejection.

Shireman hopes colleges and accreditors that are in that situation, as well as those not yet affected, are working to be proactive.

“Seeing all of what’s happening right now at the Department of Education with accrediting agencies,” he said, “I would not be surprised if professions start planning ahead, identifying and taking steps to protect against having some period where people can’t get a license.”

title: Failure to Measure Learning Is Hurting Higher Education
summary:
Failure to Measure Learning Is Hurting Higher Education
Doug Lederman Mon, 08/31/2026 - 03:00 AM

The public doubts the value of what colleges are providing. That could change if institutions proved that students actually develop the capabilities and skills we promise them.

Byline(s)
Doug Lederman
full_text:
Over the last few weeks, I’ve talked to some of the sharpest people I know about a topic that’s been troubling me.

It’s this: After decades covering higher education, and now doing what I can to help figure out how the industry can win back public trust, I’ve concluded that colleges and universities collectively are unable—or have declined—to measure and prove whether and how much their students learn.

As a result, we lack tangible, direct and incontrovertible proof that colleges and universities actually help learners develop the capabilities, skills and habits of mind that the institutions purport to deliver.

Why does that matter? Well, it’s hard to persuade people that your primary “product” is worth paying for when you can’t prove they’re actually getting it. That’s going to get even harder as AI continues to scramble our sense of what knowledge and skills are going to matter going forward.

I’m not saying I don’t believe learning happens in college: I have a lifetime of anecdotal and personal evidence from the many people I’ve seen grow and thrive after being at our institutions, and there’s no shortage of data that shows the economic, health, civic and other benefits that college-goers collectively display.

But believing (and asserting with authority, which is what college and university leaders do best) is different from knowing (in your heart and in your head, as I suspect many of you do). And knowing is different from proving.

Higher ed never really had to prove itself. Through the 1970s, at least, most people took for granted the wisdom of going to college, especially those fortunate enough to go, but even many Americans who strove to be among them (or for their kids to be).

To the extent evidence for the benefits of college was sought or put forward, it consisted mostly of the “million-dollar premium” in lifetime earnings that economists showed accrued to those with a degree over those who lacked one.

Because higher education got the public’s benefit of the doubt, institutions, individually and collectively, never really felt significant pressure to prove themselves. That was especially true of the colleges and universities that the public (and journalists and politicians, their narrators) widely presumed to be the best. You know the ones—those that have lasted the longest, enrolled the students with the highest test scores and grades, had the most esteemed professors, and topped the U.S. News rankings (based heavily on indicators like those).

Doubts always nagged, though, accelerating periodically when recessions hit, job markets tightened, government spending or student debt spiked, or Americans (or their self-appointed spokespeople, politicians and journalists) otherwise started wondering whether college was really “worth it” for individuals.

There’ve been a handful of crucible moments—the culture-war critiques of Bill Bennett, Allan Bloom and Dinesh D’Souza in the 1980s, the push for student learning outcomes by then–Education Secretary Margaret Spellings’s Commission on the Future of Higher Education in the mid-2000s, and the post–Great Recession debt concerns that were accompanied by the publication of Academically Adrift. None was as serious as the crisis of confidence today.

Lacking actual data on what and how much students learn and grow, politicians and policymakers have opted to rely on proxies they can measure, like postcollege earnings, to try to gauge postsecondary quality and success, even though they are reductionist and ignore many other contributions a higher education makes for individuals and society.

Imperfect as they are, that data tells a story of most programs at most institutions surpassing the very low floor of leaving graduates better off than peers with only a high school diploma—but with enormous variation by job field, academic discipline, race and other demographic traits, region, and institution. This data has reinforced rather than resolved the public’s doubts.

And I’m increasingly convinced that unless and until we can prove to prospective students and their families, employers and governments that colleges and universities are really arming learners with the capabilities they say they do, higher education won’t win back hearts and minds (and tuition dollars).

I plan to return to this topic in the coming weeks, to dig further into how we got here, talk about the all-important question of what it is that we should be trying to measure (a hint: For me, it’s about “durable skills” that might remain vital, no matter what AI or any other technology ultimately throw at us), explore promising approaches to how we might measure, and share thoughts from smart people like Richard Arum, Tim Knowles, Kate McConnell, Johann Neem and Hollis Robbins (and some of you?). Please write about these issues.

I hope you’ll come touch the third rail with me.

title: ED Awards TRIO Grants to Hundreds of Colleges
summary:
ED Awards TRIO Grants to Hundreds of Colleges
Olivia.sanchez Mon, 08/31/2026 - 03:00 AM

The announcement brings some relief to advocates who worried TRIO money would be rerouted to states and workforce pathway initiatives.

Byline(s)
Olivia Sanchez
full_text:
The Department of Education announced more than $186 million in federal college-access funding on Friday, easing concerns that the agency would redirect the money or not award grants at all.

Many colleges and universities are among the 326 entities that received a portion of the $142.5 million awarded to TRIO Talent Search grants, according to a list of the first slate of awardees provided by the Council for Opportunity in Education. The Department also awarded $44.7 million in TRIO Educational Opportunity Center grants to 102 entities.

Between the two programs, the department has until the end of September to announce a second slate of additional awardees.

The announcement brings relief for education advocates worried by the administration’s calls for grant proposals published earlier this year, which said states that applied for Talent Search grants would be eligible for far more money than individual institutions. Educators were also concerned that Educational Opportunity Centers grants would be redirected to workforce-pathway programs.

The Trump administration eliminated funding for TRIO programs in previous budget proposals and terminated more than 120 TRIO grants last year, further driving fears around the future of the programs.

Kimberly Jones, president of the Council for Opportunity in Education, said the initial lists of awards brings “both relief and heartbreak to the TRIO community,” because fewer total grants have been awarded so far.

“We are grateful that the Department ultimately followed the direction of Congress and that hundreds of Talent Search and EOC programs will continue serving students and families,” Jones said in a statement.

Despite the awards, other previous grant recipients are still losing services under the administration’s new funding approach, she said. “The Department made fundamental changes to these competitions that reduced the number of awards and shifted resources away from many proven programs. For the students and communities affected, those decisions have very real consequences.”

Amanda Fuchs Miller, president of Seventh Street Strategies and a former deputy assistant secretary for higher ed programs during the Biden administration, warned against drawing too many conclusions from the initial slate of funding, but from what she’s seen so far, she said it seems like the department is on track to award close to as many grants as it has historically given out, including to many institutions that previously received awards.

“Ultimately, the way this grant is structured is per student. So, if we care about how many students are benefiting from these services, which are critical … then it doesn’t matter how many grantees there are as long as the department is giving out all the money so that the grantees can do great things to make sure all students have access and can be successful in their postsecondary education,” Fuchs Miller said.

In total, more than 80 percent of the grantees announced so far for both the Talent Search and Educational Opportunity Centers programs are colleges and universities.

The average annual grant amount for the Talent Search program—which aims to increase the number of students from disadvantaged backgrounds who apply to, enroll in and graduate from college—is roughly $437,000, up from $350,000 in the previous grant cycle. This year, the largest annual awards are $10 million for the Executive Office of the State of Ohio and $5.3 million for the Wisconsin Department of Public Instruction. The remaining 324 entities received $1 million or less per year.

Educational Opportunity Centers grants, which are meant to increase the number of adults in college, averaged roughly $439,000. Of the 102 new grants, the largest awards are $3 million for the West Virginia Council for Community and Technical College Education and $2.9 million for the Oklahoma Employment Security Commission.

Zachary Jenkins, director of a Talent Search program at Marshall University, said the institution received a $625,000 annual grant—the full amount it applied for. He said he was glad to see that the grant program had not been restructured as anticipated.
